rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Test temperature-dependent selectivity in the tightly clustered early peaks while keeping gradient effects fixed. Higher temperature should also create time headroom for a shallower gradient if needed.

Keep the favorable temperature and reduce gradient steepness to test whether the remaining critical pair reaches R ≥ 1.5. The current last-peak time provides nearly two minutes of headroom before the time penalty begins.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient at the same temperature. This will reveal whether its improvement outweighs compression of the neighboring pair while further shortening elution time.

Slope changes alone have not resolved the remaining pair, so probe temperature selectivity at 55 °C. Use the 12-minute gradient to retain separation headroom for the neighboring pair while staying comfortably below the time-penalty threshold.
Return to 60 °C and test a higher starting organic fraction to change selectivity in the unresolved early cluster. This probes a different lever from gradient slope while also shortening retention.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep the starting composition and temperature fixed to test whether the critical pairs retain R ≥ 1.5.

Shorten by another grid step to locate the speed limit for full resolution at this gradient window. Injection 7 remains the faster confirmed maximum-score method if either critical pair drops below R = 1.5.

Narrow the gradient window to recover the small resolution deficits at eight minutes while keeping the last peak inside the gradient. This slope lies between injections 7 and 8 and may deliver full resolution faster than injection 7.

Test whether one step higher starting organic shortens the run while preserving full resolution. The slightly shallower slope may help the critical cluster, but this injection will check whether compression of the early peaks offsets that benefit.

Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. Explore the low-temperature selectivity regime, where reordered early peaks may separate better, using a steep gradient to limit the added retention time.

Return to the successful high-temperature selectivity and trim the gradient endpoint to just above the last peak’s estimated elution composition. This shortens the programmed gradient while making its slope slightly shallower than injection 9, aiming to preserve maximum CRF with a little more resolution margin.

Raise the endpoint one grid step to test a slope just steeper than the fastest confirmed fully resolved method. This should shorten last-peak retention, with the critical R = 1.53 pair from injection 12 defining whether full resolution survives.

Test whether a modest temperature reduction restores separation of the compressed early pair at the higher starting organic fraction. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; injection 13 has a small resolution deficit despite its rounded CRF of 1.000.

At the higher starting composition, test whether a shallower gradient restores the early pair while retaining the improved separation of its neighbor. This seeks another fully resolved method with greater resolution margin, while injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed option.

With maximum CRF secured, test a shallower gradient at the successful starting composition to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the intermediate starting composition at the same slope as injection 9 to isolate its effect on early-cluster selectivity. This checks whether a better balance between the two critical pairs could support subsequent gradient acceleration.

Back off slightly from injection 9’s near-threshold slope to seek a faster alternative to injection 7 with a little more critical-pair resolution margin than injection 9. The starting composition and temperature remain at their best demonstrated settings.

Slightly steepen the fully resolved higher-starting-organic method from injection 15 and trim its endpoint to shorten the programmed gradient. This tests the resolution boundary for that alternative while retaining injection 9 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a different selectivity regime by combining lower temperature with a higher starting organic fraction to offset added retention. This checks for an alternative fast separation rather than further refining the well-mapped 60 °C boundary.

Return to the proven high-temperature region and test a slope between injections 6 and 7. This should preserve maximum CRF with more resolution margin than the fastest method, while eluting sooner than injection 6.

Test the remaining endpoint step between injections 8 and 9 to complete the local speed-versus-resolution boundary. It may shorten elution slightly, although the critical pair is likely to fall just below 1.5; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

The faster endpoint settings have crossed the resolution boundary, so refine within the maximum-score region. This intermediate slope should provide more critical-pair margin than injection 9 while eluting sooner than injection 21.

Slightly steepen injection 19’s gradient to test the fastest fully resolved boundary at the higher starting organic fraction. The critical pair was at R = 1.52, so this small slope increase may shorten retention while preserving maximum CRF.

Use the final injection to test a trimmed gradient expected to retain maximum CRF with more critical-pair margin than injection 9 and all peaks eluting during the gradient. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, with the last peak at 6.04 minutes.
